summary: ARES: The Last Signal is a browser-based Mars survival game for children aged 7 to 12, built around one idea: every choice is connected to the next one. The player commands a Mars outpost for 30 days after a dust storm breaks its antenna. Each decision spends Power, Life Support, Radiation Safety or crew morale, and the effects carry forward. Some hit the same day. Others return days later, like a dust-clogged air filter or a drained battery. The resources you have left decide whether you can repair the antenna and which of three endings you reach. Children learn real Mars science by seeing how one decision shapes the whole mission.
details:
The core idea: connected consequences
Real Mars missions work like a chain. Power decides whether heaters, air systems and the radio can run. Air and food affect the crew’s health and mood. A tired crew makes mistakes in repairs. ARES turns that chain into the game. Nothing stands alone: every choice changes a resource, every resource limits the next choice, and everything leads to the final outcome.

The mission
The outpost ARES-1 has lost its main antenna. The crew can hear Earth but cannot reply. The goal is to survive 30 sols (Mars days) and send one last signal home. A repair tracker shows the path: find the damage, build spare parts, test the motor, turn the dish toward Earth (Sol 21), and send the signal (Sol 30). Every event in between decides what shape the crew and outpost are in when those last two steps arrive.

How choices connect

  • Daily meals: each morning the commander picks a full meal, half meal or snack bar. Full meals protect morale but use Life Support. Smaller meals save Life Support but lower morale.
  • Morale feeds back into resources: a tired, unhappy crew wastes Power each night, and at very low morale the crew can break down. A low-morale crew also makes the Sol 21 antenna alignment more expensive.
  • Delayed consequences: a quick brush of the dust-covered suit clogs the air filters three days later. Ignoring a temperature drop costs Life Support later. Pushing a frozen rover battery drains Power two sols after. The game reminds the player with “Remember Sol 8?” so the link between cause and effect is clear.
  • Choices that pay off later: studying the dust instead of just brushing it costs Power now but gives it back. Taking a research sample lifts morale and counts as a mission objective.
  • Shared resources: the same four meters pay for the solar storm response, the shield wall, the antenna repair and the final message, so spending early limits what is left at the end.

How it leads to different outcomes
The ending is decided at Sol 30 by the antenna, the final resources and the mission objectives completed:

  • Beyond the Silence: the signal is sent, all resources are healthy, morale is good, and major objectives are done.
  • A Costly Success: Earth hears the signal, but something was sacrificed, for example a short message that loses the science data.
  • Mission Interrupted: the antenna was never aligned or the resources ran out, so the plan stops. Nobody is hurt.

Eating full meals every day nearly empties Life Support, and cutting meals drains morale. In our simulated playthroughs, a careful commander reaches the best ending, and a careless one is interrupted. There is no single right answer, only trade-offs.

Built on real science
Each event is a fictional scenario inspired by a real Mars challenge, so the resource it costs matches the real problem:

  • Dust on panels: less sunlight means less Power.
  • Solar storm: radiation from the Sun means Radiation Safety drops.
  • Frozen battery: cold drains batteries, which costs Power.
  • Vanishing air: habitat air must be checked, which costs Life Support.
  • Radio silence and ghost message: communication delays between Earth and Mars.
  • Aiming the dish: radio dishes must point precisely.

After each decision, a short science note explains why it happened. [Add the NASA resources and sources you used here.]

What children learn

  • Science: Mars conditions, solar power, radiation, cold and communication delay.
  • Engineering: managing limited resources and fixing systems.
  • Thinking: planning ahead, understanding that actions have consequences, and deciding without full information.

At the end, players answer four reflection questions about their hardest choices and lessons, and can print a mission journal.

How it is built

  • Plain HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no framework and no backend.
  • One shared game state feeds every system, so a choice always updates the same meters, the story and the ending logic together.
  • Events, effects and science notes live in data files, so new events are easy to add.
  • No accounts, no personal data, and it works offline.
